answers.question: What is the difference between smoke testing (a quick "is the build even testable" check of critical paths), sanity testing (a narrow check that a specific fix/area works), and regression testing (re-running a broad suite to confirm existing behavior still works), and where does each run in a CI/CD pipeline (smoke on every build/deploy gate, sanity after a targeted change, regression before release)?
answers.shortTitle: Difference between smoke, sanity, and regression testing and where each runs in CI/CD

s1_definition.profdef: Smoke, sanity, and regression are three testing scopes that differ by breadth and intent. Smoke testing is a shallow but wide check that the most critical paths of a freshly deployed build work at all, so it decides whether the build is even worth testing further. Sanity testing is a narrow, deep check that one specific change or bug fix actually behaves correctly, without re-testing unrelated areas. Regression testing is a broad suite re-run across existing features to confirm that a change did not break previously working behavior. In a CI/CD pipeline, smoke runs as a fast gate on every build and deployment, sanity runs immediately after a targeted change, and the full regression suite runs before a release to production.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India just installed a new version of its online banking system overnight. Before letting customers in, a staff member logs in, checks a balance, and makes one small transfer to confirm the lights are on and the doors open; that quick "is it alive" check is smoke testing. Later a developer fixes only the funds-transfer screen, so a tester checks just that screen thoroughly to confirm the fix works, without re-checking loans and statements; that focused check is sanity testing. Finally, before the bank announces the release to all customers, the whole bank is tested end to end, transfers, loans, statements, cards, to be sure the new change did not silently break anything that used to work; that complete re-check is regression testing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Smoke is a wide-but-shallow "is the build alive" gate on every deploy, sanity is a narrow-but-deep check that one change works, and regression is a broad re-run that confirms old behavior still works before release.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Smoke, sanity, and regression are three testing scopes that differ by breadth and intent. Smoke testing is a shallow but wide check that the most critical paths of a freshly deployed build work at all, so it decides whether the build is even worth testing further. Sanity testing is a narrow, deep check that one specific change or bug fix actually behaves correctly, without re-testing unrelated areas. Regression testing is a broad suite re-run across existing features to confirm that a change did not break previously working behavior. In a CI/CD pipeline, smoke runs as a fast gate on every build and deployment, sanity runs immediately after a targeted change, and the full regression suite runs before a release to production.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India just installed a new version of its online banking system overnight. Before letting customers in, a staff member logs in, checks a balance, and makes one small transfer to confirm the lights are on and the doors open; that quick "is it alive" check is smoke testing. Later a developer fixes only the funds-transfer screen, so a tester checks just that screen thoroughly to confirm the fix works, without re-checking loans and statements; that focused check is sanity testing. Finally, before the bank announces the release to all customers, the whole bank is tested end to end, transfers, loans, statements, cards, to be sure the new change did not silently break anything that used to work; that complete re-check is regression testing.

**One line to remember:** Smoke is a wide-but-shallow "is the build alive" gate on every deploy, sanity is a narrow-but-deep check that one change works, and regression is a broad re-run that confirms old behavior still works before release.

sections.s2_technical:
Smoke testing, sometimes called build verification testing, is the first thing you run against a new build. It touches many critical features but only lightly, confirming that the application starts, the main screens load, authentication works, and the core happy-path flows do not immediately fail. The purpose is a fast reject: if smoke fails, there is no point running the expensive full suite, so you fail the pipeline early and send the build back. Smoke suites are intentionally small and fast, often a handful of tests that run in a minute or two, because they gate every single build and deployment. In code terms you might tag them so the runner can select only them, for example in Playwright you would tag a test with `@smoke` and run `npx playwright test --grep @smoke` so only critical-path checks execute.

Sanity testing is narrow and deep. After a specific bug fix or a small feature change, you do not want to re-run everything; you want to confirm that the changed area now behaves correctly and that its immediate neighbors still make sense. For example, if a developer fixed a rounding bug in interest calculation, a sanity check exercises several interest scenarios in depth, boundary amounts, zero balance, large balance, but does not re-test the card module. Sanity testing is often unscripted or lightly scripted and is a subset chosen by judgement, whereas smoke is a fixed predefined set. The distinction interviewers want is that smoke is breadth-first and shallow across the whole system, while sanity is depth-first and narrow on one change.

Regression testing is the broad safety net. Any change, even a correct one, can have side effects elsewhere, because code is interconnected. Regression re-runs a large suite of previously passing tests across many features to catch those unintended side effects. Because this suite is large and slow, you automate as much of it as possible and run it at the right pipeline stage, typically before a release or nightly, rather than on every commit. In a CI/CD pipeline the placement matters: smoke runs on every build and right after each deployment to an environment as a gate; sanity runs right after a targeted change, often by the developer or in the feature branch pipeline; and the full regression suite runs in the pre-release stage, for example against a staging environment before promoting to production. A senior nuance is that these are scopes, not tools, so the same automation framework can hold all three, and you organize them with tags and pipeline stages. Another nuance is that smoke and sanity are sometimes conflated in casual usage, but the precise difference is breadth versus depth: smoke is wide and shallow to accept or reject the build, sanity is narrow and deep to validate a specific change.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India deploys a new build of its online banking service several times a day. If a build is fundamentally broken, running the full two-hour regression suite on it wastes everyone's time and blocks the pipeline. The bank needs a fast gate that quickly answers "is this build even worth testing?" This is exactly what a smoke suite does: a few critical-path checks that run in under two minutes and fail the pipeline immediately if the build cannot even log in or show a balance.

Problem 2 — A developer fixes only the funds-transfer rounding logic. Re-running every test is wasteful, but shipping the fix untested is risky. The bank needs a focused, deep check of just the transfer area. This is exactly what sanity testing does: narrow but thorough validation of the changed feature.

Problem 3 — Before announcing a release to all customers, the bank must be sure the change did not break loans, statements, or cards. This is exactly regression testing: a broad re-run of previously passing tests.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models a test runner which can execute three named suites, smoke, sanity, and regression, against a small banking system with login, transfer, loan, and statement features. We define a `BankingSystem` with those operations, a `TestCase` with a name and a scope tag, a `TestRunner` that filters and runs cases by scope and reports pass or fail counts, and a `TestingStrategyDemo` main class that runs smoke first as a gate, then sanity on the transfer change, then the full regression suite, printing where each belongs in the pipeline.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fresh build of the banking system with login and transfer healthy, and a test catalog containing two smoke, two sanity, and four regression cases.

Step 1: CI stage one runs the smoke scope. The runner filters the catalog to the two cases tagged SMOKE and executes them. The data here is just pass or fail booleans from the system's critical paths.

Step 2: Both smoke checks pass, so the gate opens and the pipeline proceeds. If either had failed, the runner would return false, the demo would log a severe message, and the pipeline would stop here without running anything expensive.

Step 3: CI stage two runs the sanity scope on the transfer change. The runner executes the two SANITY cases in depth, a positive transfer of fifty thousand rupees and a zero-amount transfer that must be rejected. The zero case passes because the system correctly refuses a non-positive amount.

Step 4: CI stage three runs the full regression scope. The runner executes all four REGRESSION cases across login, transfer, loan, and statement, confirming no feature regressed.

Step 5: The runner reports pass counts per scope. The final output shows each stage and whether it passed, mirroring how a real pipeline gates on smoke and only reaches regression before release.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Smoke, sanity, and regression are three testing scopes that differ by breadth and by intent. Smoke testing is a wide but shallow check of the most critical paths of a freshly deployed build; its only job is to answer "is this build even worth testing?" so it runs as a fast gate on every build and deployment and fails the pipeline early if the application cannot even start, log in, or perform a core action. Sanity testing is the opposite shape, narrow but deep; after a specific fix or small change I check just that area thoroughly, without re-testing unrelated features, so it runs right after a targeted change. Regression testing is the broad safety net that re-runs a large suite of previously passing tests across many features to catch unintended side effects, and because it is slow I run it in the pre-release stage, typically against staging before promoting to production, or nightly.

The way I keep these straight is to remember that smoke is breadth-first and shallow to accept or reject the build, sanity is depth-first and narrow to validate one change, and regression is broad to protect existing behavior. They are scopes, not tools, so one automation framework holds all three, and I organize them with tags and pipeline stages rather than separate projects.

At the National Bank of India I built exactly this layering. Our online banking service deployed several times a day, so I tagged a tiny smoke suite of login, balance, and a one-rupee transfer that ran in under two minutes and gated every deployment; if smoke failed we rejected the build immediately instead of wasting an hour on the full suite. When a developer fixed only the interest-rounding logic, I ran a focused sanity pass over several interest scenarios including boundary amounts, without touching cards or loans. Then before each release I ran the complete regression suite against staging, covering transfers, loans, statements, and cards, to be sure the change had not broken anything that previously worked. Being able to explain not just the definitions but exactly where each sits in the pipeline, smoke as the per-deploy gate, sanity after a targeted change, and regression before release, is what shows an interviewer I have actually designed a testing strategy rather than memorized three words.

answers.question: What is the difference between functional and non-functional testing, and where do unit, integration, system/end-to-end, and acceptance testing sit in the test pyramid (many fast unit tests at the base, fewer slow E2E tests at the top), and why is an "ice-cream cone" (mostly manual/E2E) an anti-pattern?
answers.shortTitle: Functional vs non-functional testing, the test pyramid, and why the ice-cream cone is an anti-pattern

s1_definition.profdef: Functional testing verifies what the system does, that each feature produces the correct output for a given input against the requirements. Non-functional testing verifies how well the system does it, covering performance, scalability, security, reliability, usability, and similar quality attributes. The test pyramid is a strategy for distributing tests by level: a wide base of many fast, cheap unit tests, a middle layer of fewer integration tests, and a narrow top of a small number of slow, expensive system and end-to-end tests, with acceptance tests validating business requirements. The ice-cream cone is the inverted anti-pattern where most testing is slow manual or end-to-end checks and few unit tests exist, which is slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, functional testing asks "does the transfer actually move fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya correctly?" Non-functional testing asks "can the transfer system handle ten thousand transfers per second during salary day, stay secure, and respond within one hundred milliseconds?" The test pyramid is like quality checks in the bank: thousands of tiny instant checks on each calculation at the base, fewer checks that two departments talk correctly in the middle, and a handful of full dress-rehearsals of a complete customer journey at the top. The ice-cream cone is the bad bank that skips the tiny checks and instead does only expensive full dress-rehearsals by hand, so every tiny bug is caught slowly, late, and at great cost.
s1_definition.oneliner: Functional testing checks what the system does and non-functional checks how well it does it; put many fast unit tests at the base of the pyramid and few slow end-to-end tests at the top, never the inverted ice-cream cone of mostly manual end-to-end checks.

**One line to remember:** Functional testing checks what the system does and non-functional checks how well it does it; put many fast unit tests at the base of the pyramid and few slow end-to-end tests at the top, never the inverted ice-cream cone of mostly manual end-to-end checks.

sections.s2_technical:
Functional testing is requirement-driven. For every feature you confirm that given a specific input, the system produces the expected output and the expected side effects. In a banking app, functional tests confirm that a transfer debits one account, credits another, records an audit entry, and returns a success response. Functional testing spans all levels, you can test a function, a service, or the whole system functionally, so functional versus non-functional is about intent, not level.

Non-functional testing targets quality attributes rather than specific features. Performance testing measures response time and throughput under load; scalability testing measures how the system behaves as load grows; security testing probes for vulnerabilities; reliability and endurance testing look for memory leaks and failures over sustained use; usability and accessibility testing assess the experience. These do not ask "is the answer correct" but "is it fast, safe, stable, and usable enough."

The test pyramid describes the healthy distribution of tests by level. At the base are unit tests: they test one class or function in isolation, run in milliseconds, need no database or network, and are cheap to write and maintain, so you have thousands of them. Above them are integration tests: they verify that components work together, for example a service plus its repository against a real or in-memory database, slower and fewer. Near the top are system and end-to-end tests: they drive the whole deployed application through its real interfaces, a browser clicking through a transfer, which are slow, flaky-prone, and expensive, so you keep them few and reserve them for the most critical journeys. Acceptance tests sit at the business-requirement level, often written with stakeholders, confirming the system satisfies agreed behavior, and are frequently expressed as end-to-end or close to it.

The ice-cream cone is the pyramid flipped upside down: a huge blob of manual testing on top, many end-to-end tests below it, and almost no unit tests at the bottom. It is an anti-pattern because end-to-end tests are slow, so feedback takes hours instead of seconds; they are brittle, because a tiny UI change breaks many of them; they are expensive to maintain; and when one fails it is hard to localize the defect because so much code is exercised at once. With few unit tests, bugs that a fast unit test would have caught in milliseconds instead surface late in a slow end-to-end run or in manual testing, which is the most expensive place to find them. The senior framing is that you want fast, localized feedback at the base and only a thin, carefully chosen layer of slow, broad checks at the top, so defects are caught as early and as cheaply as possible, and the suite stays fast and stable enough to run on every commit.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs to know its transfer logic is correct at the smallest level, for example that debiting an account reduces the balance and rejects an overdraft, without spinning up a database or a browser. This is exactly what unit tests do: fast, isolated checks of one piece of logic.

Problem 2 — The bank also needs to know the service and repository cooperate, that saving a transfer actually persists both account changes together. This is exactly what integration tests do.

Problem 3 — The bank needs to confirm the full customer journey works through the real interface, log in, transfer, see the new balance. This is exactly what an end-to-end test does, and because it is slow and broad, there should be only a few of these.

Problem 4 — The bank must also confirm the transfer is fast enough under load; that correctness question is non-functional, measured separately.

In the mini-project we model the pyramid by categorizing tests by level and counting them, demonstrating the healthy shape, and we include one non-functional check that measures elapsed time against an SLA. We define an `AccountService` with transfer logic, a `LeveledTest` with a level tag (UNIT, INTEGRATION, E2E, ACCEPTANCE) and whether it is functional or non-functional, and a `PyramidAnalyzer` that counts tests per level and warns if the distribution looks like an ice-cream cone.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a catalog of nine tests, four unit, two integration, two end-to-end plus acceptance, and one non-functional performance check.

Step 1: The demo runs each test and records pass or fail. Unit tests execute instantly in memory with no database, demonstrating the cheap fast base.

Step 2: Integration tests run next, exercising the service across two operations, slightly broader and slower in a real system.

Step 3: The end-to-end and acceptance tests run, representing the full journey; in a real system these drive a browser and take seconds each.

Step 4: The non-functional performance test measures elapsed milliseconds for a transfer and compares it to a one-hundred-millisecond SLA, asking "how fast," not "is it correct."

Step 5: The PyramidAnalyzer counts tests per level and checks the shape. Because there are far more unit tests than end-to-end tests, it reports a healthy pyramid rather than an ice-cream cone.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Functional testing verifies what the system does, that each feature returns the correct result and side effects for a given input against the requirements, while non-functional testing verifies how well it does it, covering performance, scalability, security, reliability, and usability. The two are about intent, not level, so I can test functionally or non-functionally at any layer.

The test pyramid is how I distribute tests by level for the best feedback. At the base I put many fast, isolated unit tests that run in milliseconds with no database or network; above them a smaller set of integration tests that confirm components cooperate, for example a service with its repository and database; and at the narrow top only a few slow, broad system and end-to-end tests that drive the whole deployed application through its real interface, with acceptance tests validating agreed business behavior. The ice-cream cone is this shape flipped upside down, mostly manual and end-to-end checks with almost no unit tests, and it is an anti-pattern because end-to-end tests are slow so feedback takes hours, brittle so a small UI change breaks many of them, expensive to maintain, and poor at localizing a defect because they exercise so much code at once; meanwhile bugs that a unit test would catch in milliseconds instead surface late and expensively.

At the National Bank of India I deliberately built a pyramid. Our transfer and interest logic had thousands of unit tests with JUnit and Mockito running on every commit in seconds; a focused layer of integration tests used Testcontainers against a real PostgreSQL to confirm service and repository persisted both account changes atomically; and a thin top of Playwright end-to-end tests covered only the critical journeys, login, transfer, and balance. Separately I ran a non-functional track with JMeter to confirm transfers stayed under our one-hundred-millisecond SLA at ten thousand requests per second on salary day, and security scans for vulnerabilities. When I joined, one team had an ice-cream cone with mostly manual end-to-end testing and a two-hour feedback loop; by pushing coverage down to fast unit tests I cut feedback to under five minutes and made the suite stable enough to gate every commit. Being able to explain what each level is for and why the pyramid shape matters is what shows an interviewer I design test strategy for fast, cheap, early feedback rather than piling everything into slow end-to-end checks.

answers.question: What is the difference between severity (the technical/business IMPACT of a defect) and priority (how URGENTLY it must be fixed), and why can a defect be low-severity but high-priority (e.g. a company-logo typo on the landing page) or high-severity but low-priority (a crash in a rarely-used admin edge case)?
answers.shortTitle: Severity vs priority, and why they can diverge

s1_definition.profdef: Severity is the degree of technical and business impact a defect has on the system, how badly it breaks functionality, data, or safety, and it is usually judged by the tester or by the nature of the bug. Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to other work, judged by the product owner or business based on customer, revenue, reputational, and scheduling factors. They are independent axes, so a defect can be any combination of high or low on each: a defect can be low-severity but high-priority, such as a misspelled company name on the landing page, or high-severity but low-priority, such as a crash in a rarely used admin edge case affecting one internal user.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, severity is "how much damage does this bug do?" and priority is "how soon must we fix it?" A typo in the bank's name splashed across the public homepage does almost no technical damage, so it is low severity, but it embarrasses the brand in front of every visitor, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making it high priority. On the other hand, a rare crash deep inside an admin screen that only one back-office clerk ever opens is technically a serious crash, high severity, but because almost nobody hits it and there is a manual workaround, the business is fine fixing it next sprint, making it low priority.
s1_definition.oneliner: Severity measures how badly a defect damages the system, priority measures how urgently it must be fixed, and because impact and urgency are different axes a bug can be low-severity high-priority, like a homepage typo, or high-severity low-priority, like a crash in a rarely used admin corner.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, severity is "how much damage does this bug do?" and priority is "how soon must we fix it?" A typo in the bank's name splashed across the public homepage does almost no technical damage, so it is low severity, but it embarrasses the brand in front of every visitor, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making it high priority. sections.s2_technical:
Severity is primarily a technical judgement about the defect itself. A crash, data corruption, a wrong monetary calculation, or a security hole are high severity because they damage core functionality, correctness, or safety. A cosmetic misalignment, a non-blocking warning, or a minor label issue is low severity because the system still works correctly. Teams usually define severity levels such as critical, major, minor, and trivial, with objective criteria so testers can classify consistently. Severity tends to be set by whoever finds and analyzes the bug, because it reflects the nature of the failure.

Priority is a business and scheduling judgement about when to fix it. It weighs how many users are affected, whether there is a workaround, the revenue or compliance impact, reputational risk, the release schedule, and what else is competing for developer time. Priority is usually set by the product owner or triage group, often in collaboration with the tester. The same defect can have its priority raised or lowered as business context changes, for example a bug becomes high priority the week before a major launch.

The two diverge because impact and urgency are different questions. The classic low-severity, high-priority case is a typo in the company name or a wrong logo on the public landing page: technically nothing is broken, the system works perfectly, so severity is low, yet every visitor sees an embarrassing brand mistake, so the business demands an immediate fix, making priority high. The classic high-severity, low-priority case is a crash in a rarely used administrative edge case: a crash is a serious failure, so severity is high, but perhaps only one internal user ever triggers it, a manual workaround exists, and no customer or money is affected, so the business is comfortable scheduling it for a later sprint, making priority low. Other combinations are common too: a high-severity high-priority bug is a transfer that debits the wrong amount, fix now; a low-severity low-priority bug is a cosmetic misalignment on a seldom-visited settings page, fix whenever convenient.

The senior nuances are these. First, keep the axes separate in your tracker with two distinct fields, because conflating them leads to poor triage, either polishing cosmetic issues while serious bugs wait, or ignoring a scary-sounding bug that does not actually matter. Second, severity informs priority but does not determine it; the business decides priority using severity as one input among many. Third, always capture a workaround and the affected user population in the bug report, because those are exactly the facts that let a product owner set priority correctly. Fourth, be ready in an interview to defend a surprising combination with a concrete example, because that is how an interviewer checks you truly understand the distinction rather than treating the two words as synonyms.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's public homepage shows the bank name misspelled. Nothing is technically broken, but every visitor sees it, so the brand team wants it fixed immediately. The bank needs a way to record that this defect has low technical impact but high business urgency. This is exactly a low-severity, high-priority defect.

Problem 2 — A crash occurs in a rarely used admin report that one back-office clerk opens once a month, and there is a manual workaround. The crash is technically serious but almost nobody hits it. This is exactly a high-severity, low-priority defect.

Problem 3 — A transfer occasionally debits the wrong amount. This damages money and must be fixed now, a high-severity, high-priority defect, so the bank needs triage logic that treats this as the most urgent.

In the mini-project we build a defect triage model that stores severity and priority as separate fields, computes a triage recommendation, and sorts the defect queue so that business priority drives the fix order while severity is preserved for engineering context. We define a `Severity` enum, a `Priority` enum, a `Defect` with both fields plus affected-user count and workaround flag, and a `TriageService` that sorts by priority and explains each surprising combination.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Severity and priority are two independent axes of a defect. Severity is the technical and business impact, how badly the defect breaks functionality, correctness, data, or safety, and it is normally set by the tester based on the nature of the failure. Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to everything else, and it is normally set by the product owner based on how many users are affected, whether there is a workaround, revenue and compliance impact, reputation, and the release schedule. Because impact and urgency are different questions, the two can point in opposite directions.

The classic low-severity, high-priority example is a misspelled company name or a wrong logo on the public landing page: technically nothing is broken so severity is trivial, but every visitor sees an embarrassing brand mistake, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making priority the highest. The mirror image is a crash in a rarely used admin edge case: a crash is technically serious so severity is critical, but if only one internal user ever triggers it and a manual workaround exists, the business is comfortable scheduling it for a later sprint, so priority is low. Of course many bugs are aligned, a transfer debiting the wrong amount is both high severity and high priority and must be fixed immediately, while a cosmetic misalignment on a seldom-visited page is low on both.

At the National Bank of India I always kept the two as separate fields in the tracker, and in bug reports I captured the affected-user count and whether a workaround existed, because those are exactly the facts the product owner needs to set priority sensibly. I remember a release week where a homepage typo in the bank's name, technically trivial, was raised to top priority ahead of a genuinely critical but rarely hit admin crash, and being able to explain calmly why that ordering was correct, impact versus urgency, reassured the stakeholders. Keeping the axes separate stops two failure modes: polishing cosmetic issues while serious bugs wait, and panicking over a scary-sounding bug that does not actually affect anyone. Being able to defend a surprising combination with a concrete banking example is what shows an interviewer I genuinely understand the distinction rather than treating the two words as synonyms.

answers.question: Walk through the bug life cycle (New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retest → Verified → Closed) and the alternate states (Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, Deferred, Not Reproducible) — and how do you handle a bug a developer says they "cannot reproduce" (capture exact environment/version/data/steps, logs, video/screenshots, network trace, and a minimal deterministic repro)?
answers.shortTitle: The bug life cycle, alternate states, and handling a "cannot reproduce" defect

s1_definition.profdef: The bug life cycle is the sequence of states a defect moves through from discovery to closure: New when first logged, Assigned when given to a developer, Open while being worked, Fixed when the code change is done, Retest when the tester re-verifies, Verified when the fix is confirmed, and Closed when the defect is fully resolved. Alternate states handle non-linear outcomes: Reopened when a supposedly fixed bug recurs, Rejected when it is not a valid defect, Duplicate when it matches an existing bug, Deferred when a valid bug is postponed, and Not Reproducible when the developer cannot recreate it. A cannot-reproduce bug is handled by supplying the exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, video, and network trace, ideally reduced to a minimal deterministic reproduction.
s1_definition.analogy: When a teller at the National Bank of India spots a problem, say the balance screen shows a wrong figure, it starts as a New complaint. It is handed to an engineer, Assigned, who starts work, Open, makes the repair, Fixed, hands it back for the teller to re-check, Retest, the teller confirms it is correct, Verified, and the ticket is filed away, Closed. Sometimes the path bends: the problem comes back, Reopened; the engineer says it is working as designed, Rejected; someone already reported it, Duplicate; it is real but will wait until next release, Deferred; or the engineer simply cannot make it happen on their machine, Not Reproducible. For that last case, the teller must hand over the exact branch, the app version, the specific account and amounts, the precise click-by-click steps, screen recordings, and the system logs, so the engineer can finally see it happen.
s1_definition.oneliner: A bug flows New to Assigned to Open to Fixed to Retest to Verified to Closed, with alternate states Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, Deferred, and Not Reproducible, and you defeat a "cannot reproduce" by handing over exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, video, and a minimal deterministic repro.

sections.s2_technical:
The standard flow begins at New when the tester logs a defect with a clear title, steps, expected and actual results, and evidence. A triage or lead then moves it to Assigned by giving it to a developer. When the developer begins investigating, it becomes Open, sometimes called In Progress. Once the developer commits a fix, it becomes Fixed, and the build carrying that fix is deployed to a test environment. The tester then re-runs the scenario, which is the Retest state, and if the bug is gone and nothing else broke, the tester marks it Verified. Finally the defect is Closed, meaning it is fully resolved and needs no further action.

The alternate states handle real-world non-linearity. Reopened happens when a Fixed-and-closed bug recurs, often because the fix was incomplete or a regression reintroduced it; the tester reopens rather than filing a brand new bug so history is preserved. Rejected, sometimes called Not a Bug or Working as Designed, is used when the reported behavior is actually correct per the requirements or is a misunderstanding; good practice is for the developer to explain why so the tester can learn or escalate. Duplicate marks a defect that is the same underlying issue as an existing one, and you link the two so the fix on the original resolves both. Deferred marks a valid bug that the business consciously postpones, typically because it is low priority and the release cannot wait; it stays in the backlog with a reason. Not Reproducible is used when the developer cannot recreate the failure, which is where the interesting work lies.

Handling a cannot-reproduce bug well is a senior skill because non-reproducibility is usually a symptom of missing context, not a non-existent bug. The disciplined response is to gather and attach everything that could differ between the tester's and developer's worlds. That means the exact environment, operating system, browser and version, device, and which deployed environment; the exact build or version of the application and its dependencies; the exact data, the specific account identifiers, amounts, and any special state such as an account that is dormant or over a limit; the exact reproduction steps in precise order, with no assumed knowledge; and rich evidence, a screen recording or screenshots at the moment of failure, the application and server logs correlated by a request or trace identifier, and a browser network trace or HAR file showing the actual request and response. The goal is to reduce the problem to a minimal deterministic reproduction, the smallest set of steps and data that reliably triggers the failure, because determinism is what converts a hand-waving "sometimes it breaks" into a bug a developer can fix. Common hidden causes that non-reproducibility exposes are environment differences, time zone or locale, specific data states, race conditions and timing, cached state, feature flags, or an authentication and permission difference. The senior nuance is to treat Not Reproducible as a collaboration prompt rather than a dead end: you add the missing context, and if it still cannot be reproduced you instrument the code with extra logging and wait for it to recur in production with correlation identifiers, so that the next occurrence is captured with everything needed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A tester at the National Bank of India finds that a transfer shows a wrong balance, and the defect must move through clear states so everyone knows who owns it and what stage it is at. This is exactly the bug life cycle: New, Assigned, Open, Fixed, Retest, Verified, Closed.

Problem 2 — A developer marks a different bug Not Reproducible because it works on their machine. The tester must supply exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, and a trace to make it deterministic. This is exactly the cannot-reproduce workflow.

Problem 3 — Some reports are not real defects or already exist, so the model must support Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, and Deferred as valid outcomes.

In the mini-project we build a defect state machine that enforces legal transitions, records a reproduction bundle, and demonstrates resolving a Not Reproducible bug by attaching the missing context so it becomes reproducible and progresses to Fixed. We define a `BugState` enum, a `ReproBundle` capturing environment, version, data, steps, and evidence, a `Defect` holding its current state and bundle, and a `BugWorkflow` that validates transitions and logs the journey.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two defects, one a clean wrong-balance bug, one an intermittent dormant-account failure that the developer cannot reproduce.

Step 1: The happy-path defect moves New to Assigned to Open as the developer picks it up and investigates. Each transition is validated against the allowed-transitions map.

Step 2: The developer fixes it, so it moves Open to Fixed, the build deploys, and the tester re-runs it in Retest, confirms it, and marks it Verified, then Closed. The full linear journey is logged.

Step 3: The second defect moves New to Assigned to Open, but the developer cannot recreate it, so it moves Open to Not Reproducible.

Step 4: The tester tries to push it back to Open without supplying context. The workflow guard blocks the transition because the reproduction bundle is incomplete, enforcing the discipline that non-reproducibility needs more information.

Step 5: The tester attaches the complete bundle, exact environment, exact version, exact data including the dormant-over-one-hundred-eighty-days state, precise steps, and evidence including a video, a correlated server log trace identifier, and a network HAR file. Now the guard passes, the bug returns to Open, and the developer, finally able to see it deterministically, fixes it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The bug life cycle is the set of states a defect moves through from discovery to closure. It starts at New when I log it with clear steps, expected and actual results, and evidence; moves to Assigned when a developer owns it; to Open while they investigate; to Fixed when the code change lands; to Retest when I re-run the scenario against the new build; to Verified when I confirm the fix and that nothing else broke; and finally to Closed. Around that main line are the alternate states that reflect reality: Reopened when a closed bug recurs, which preserves history instead of filing a new one; Rejected when the behavior is actually correct or a misunderstanding; Duplicate when it matches an existing defect and the two are linked; Deferred when a valid bug is consciously postponed with a reason; and Not Reproducible when the developer cannot recreate it.

Handling a cannot-reproduce bug is where I show seniority, because non-reproducibility almost always means missing context rather than a non-existent bug. My response is to supply everything that could differ between my world and the developer's: the exact environment including operating system, browser, version, and which deployed environment; the exact application build; the exact data including specific account identifiers, amounts, and special states such as a dormant account; the precise ordered steps with nothing assumed; and rich evidence, a screen recording, the server and application logs correlated by a request or trace identifier, and a browser network or HAR trace. My goal is a minimal deterministic reproduction, the smallest steps and data that reliably trigger it, because determinism is what lets a developer actually fix it. If it still will not reproduce, I instrument the code with extra logging keyed by a correlation identifier and wait for the next occurrence so it is captured completely.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this discipline. We once had an intermittent debit failure that a developer marked Not Reproducible; I reproduced it only after noticing it happened only on accounts dormant for more than one hundred eighty days, so I attached that data state, the exact staging build, click-by-click steps, a screen recording, and a server log with the matching trace identifier, and the developer fixed it within the day. I also treat Not Reproducible as a collaboration prompt, not a dead end, and I always capture a workaround and the affected population in the report. Being able to walk the full life cycle including the alternate states, and to explain concretely how I turn a cannot-reproduce into a deterministic repro, is what tells an interviewer I manage defects like an experienced engineer rather than just filing tickets.

answers.shortTitle: Writing login page test cases beyond the happy path

s1_definition.profdef: Writing login test cases beyond the happy path means systematically covering the full behavior surface of authentication rather than only the one valid-credentials success flow. It includes positive cases, many negative cases such as invalid username, invalid password, both invalid, and empty fields, security behaviors such as account lockout after a threshold of failed attempts and rejection of SQL-injection and cross-site-scripting inputs, session behaviors such as remember-me, session timeout, and logout, recovery flows such as password reset, non-functional checks such as browser compatibility and accessibility, and verification of precise, non-leaky error messages. The interviewer is evaluating whether you think like a tester who anticipates how a feature fails and is abused, not merely whether login works.
s1_definition.analogy: For the National Bank of India login screen, the happy path is Rajesh typing his correct username and password and getting in. But a real tester asks all the uncomfortable questions: what if the password is wrong, what if both fields are empty, what if someone tries the wrong password ten times to break in, does the password show as dots so a shoulder-surfer cannot read it, does "remember me" actually keep him logged in, does the session expire after inactivity so an unattended machine is safe, can an attacker type a database trick or a script into the username box, and does the error message say just "invalid credentials" rather than revealing whether the username exists. Covering all of these is what separates a real tester from someone who only checks that the front door opens for the right key.
s1_definition.oneliner: Login testing beyond the happy path covers negatives, empty fields, masking, lockout, remember-me, session timeout, logout, injection and scripting attacks, password reset, browser and accessibility checks, and precise non-leaky error messages, because the interviewer is checking that you anticipate failure and abuse, not just success.

sections.s2_technical:
The happy path is a single case: valid username and valid password lead to a successful login and a redirect to the dashboard. Everything interesting is around it. The negative credential matrix covers valid username with invalid password, invalid username with any password, both invalid, and the correct rule that all failures return the same generic message so an attacker cannot tell which part was wrong, which is an account-enumeration defense. Empty-field cases cover empty username, empty password, both empty, and whitespace-only input, each expecting a clear validation message and no server call wasted.

Security behaviors are central for a bank. Account lockout after a threshold, for example five failed attempts, must lock the account for a cooldown or until reset, and you test the boundary precisely: the Nth attempt still allows, the N-plus-first triggers lockout, and a correct password during lockout is still refused. Input-injection cases feed SQL-injection payloads such as a quote-or-one-equals-one string and cross-site-scripting payloads such as a script tag into both fields, expecting the input to be safely rejected or escaped with no database error leaked and no script executed, confirming parameterized queries and output encoding. Password masking checks that the password renders as dots, that an optional show-password toggle works, and that the value is not exposed in the DOM in plain text or logged.

Session behaviors include remember-me, which should persist a secure, http-only, same-site cookie so the user stays logged in across browser restarts, and critically that it does not persist on a shared machine beyond its intended scope; session timeout, which should invalidate the session after a configured idle period and force re-authentication; and logout, which must invalidate the server session and clear cookies so the back button cannot reach an authenticated page. Recovery includes the password-reset flow, confirming a reset link is single-use and time-limited and that requesting a reset for a non-existent email does not reveal whether the account exists. Non-functional checks include browser compatibility across the supported matrix, for example Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, and accessibility, confirming the form is keyboard-navigable, has proper labels and ARIA roles, announces errors to screen readers, and meets contrast requirements. Finally, precise error messages must be user-friendly and non-leaky, never exposing stack traces, SQL errors, or whether a username exists.

The senior nuance, and what the interviewer is really assessing, is breadth of thinking and risk awareness. Anyone can test that login works. A strong tester enumerates failure modes, abuse cases, and quality attributes, prioritizes them by risk, which for a bank puts lockout, injection, session, and enumeration at the top, and writes each case with precise preconditions, steps, data, and an exact expected result including the exact message text and the security property being protected. Demonstrating that structure, grouping cases into positive, negative, security, session, recovery, and non-functional, is how you show you think past "login works."
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the login screen is the front door to everyone's money, so it must reject wrong credentials with a message that does not reveal whether the username exists. This is exactly the negative and enumeration-defense cases.

Problem 2 — Attackers will try passwords repeatedly and will paste database tricks and scripts into the fields. The system must lock the account after a threshold and safely neutralize injection and scripting input. This is exactly the lockout and injection cases.

Problem 3 — A logged-in session on an unattended machine is dangerous, so sessions must time out and logout must fully invalidate. This is exactly the session cases.

In the mini-project we model a login service that enforces these rules and a test catalog that exercises them, so the demo doubles as executable test cases. We define an `AuthResult`, a `LoginService` with generic error messages, lockout after five attempts, input sanitization, masking metadata, and session timeout, and a `LoginTestSuite` that runs positive, negative, security, and session cases and reports results.

Input data: a login service pre-loaded with Rajesh and Priya, and a suite of ten executable cases plus a note of the manual and end-to-end cases.

Step 1: The positive case logs in Rajesh with correct credentials and expects SUCCESS, confirming the happy path still works.

Step 2: The negative cases submit a wrong password for a valid user and any password for an unknown user, and both return the same generic invalid-credentials result, proving the system does not reveal whether the username exists.

Step 3: The empty-field case submits blank fields and expects a validation error before any credential check.

Step 4: The security lockout case fails four times, which are still allowed as invalid, then the fifth failure flips the account to LOCKED, and a subsequent correct password is still refused while locked, verifying the boundary exactly.

Step 5: The injection and scripting cases paste a SQL payload and a script tag, both of which the service blocks without leaking any database error, and the masking and session-timeout properties are asserted. The demo then lists the remaining manual and end-to-end cases such as remember-me, logout invalidation, single-use reset links, the browser matrix, and accessibility.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I write login test cases I start from the position that the happy path, valid username and valid password leading to the dashboard, is a single case, and that everything valuable lies around it. I group the rest into families. The negative credential matrix covers valid user with wrong password, unknown user, both invalid, and the crucial rule that every failure returns the same generic message so an attacker cannot enumerate which usernames exist. Empty-field cases cover blank and whitespace-only input with clear validation before any server call. Security cases cover account lockout after a threshold such as five attempts, tested exactly at the boundary so the fifth failure locks and a correct password is still refused while locked, and injection cases that paste SQL and cross-site-scripting payloads into both fields and expect them safely neutralized with no database error or script execution. Session cases cover remember-me using a secure, http-only, same-site cookie, session timeout after idle, and logout that fully invalidates the server session so the back button cannot reach a protected page. Recovery covers a single-use, time-limited password-reset link that does not reveal whether an email exists. Non-functional cases cover the supported browser matrix and accessibility, keyboard navigation, labels and ARIA roles, screen-reader error announcements, and contrast. And throughout I assert precise, non-leaky error messages that never expose stack traces or SQL.

What I believe the interviewer is really evaluating is whether I think past "login works." Anyone can confirm the front door opens for the right key; a strong tester enumerates how the feature fails and how it is abused, prioritizes by risk, which for a bank puts lockout, injection, session handling, and enumeration defense at the top, and writes each case with precise preconditions, data, steps, and an exact expected result including the message text and the security property being protected.

At the National Bank of India I owned the login test suite, and I caught two real issues this way: a response that revealed whether a username existed, which I flagged as an account-enumeration vulnerability, and a logout that did not invalidate the server session so the back button still showed account data. Both were missed by happy-path testing and both mattered because this was the front door to customers' money. Being able to lay out these case families and explain the risk behind each, especially the security and session ones, is exactly how I show an interviewer I test like someone who protects a bank, not someone who checks a checkbox.

answers.question: Write test cases for a payment gateway with a focus on financial correctness and reliability — success, failure, insufficient balance, invalid/expired card, wrong CVV, payment timeout, DUPLICATE payment request, network/callback failure, refund and partial refund, currency conversion, transaction-status mismatch, user closes the browser mid-payment, and the critical case where the payment SUCCEEDS but the confirmation fails — and why do idempotency and duplicate-transaction handling matter more here than UI validation?
answers.shortTitle: Writing payment gateway test cases focused on financial correctness and reliability

s1_definition.profdef: Payment gateway testing focuses on financial correctness and reliability rather than cosmetics, because a mistake moves real money. It covers the success path, declines such as insufficient balance, invalid or expired card, and wrong CVV, reliability failures such as payment timeout, network and callback failures, and the user closing the browser mid-payment, and correctness-critical flows such as duplicate payment requests, refunds and partial refunds, currency conversion, and transaction-status mismatches between the gateway and the merchant. The most important case is the payment succeeding at the gateway while the confirmation back to the merchant fails, which must never result in a double charge or a lost payment. Idempotency and duplicate-transaction handling matter more than UI validation here because retries and network failures are routine, and only an idempotency key and robust reconciliation prevent charging a customer twice.
s1_definition.analogy: When Priya pays fifty thousand rupees through the National Bank of India gateway, the tester cares less about whether the form looks nice and far more about money being exactly right. What if her card is expired, what if the network drops right after the bank charged her but before the shop heard back, what if she double-clicks pay, what if she closes the browser halfway, what if a refund is partial? The scariest case is: the bank really took her money, but the message confirming it got lost, so the shop thinks she did not pay. If the system is not careful, she gets charged twice or the shop ships nothing. The safeguard is an idempotency key, a unique ticket on the request so that even if it is sent five times, the money moves exactly once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Payment testing prioritizes money correctness and reliability, declines, timeouts, duplicates, refunds, currency, and especially payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails, and idempotency keys matter more than UI validation because retries are routine and only idempotency stops a double charge.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Priya pays fifty thousand rupees through the National Bank of India gateway, the tester cares less about whether the form looks nice and far more about money being exactly right. **One line to remember:** Payment testing prioritizes money correctness and reliability, declines, timeouts, duplicates, refunds, currency, and especially payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails, and idempotency keys matter more than UI validation because retries are routine and only idempotency stops a double charge.

sections.s2_technical:
The success path confirms a valid payment debits the payer, credits the merchant, records a transaction with a unique reference, and returns a confirmed status. Decline cases each produce a specific, safe outcome: insufficient balance must reject without partial debit; an invalid or expired card must be refused before any charge; a wrong CVV must be rejected by the processor. These are financial-correctness cases because the invariant is that a declined payment leaves balances untouched.

Reliability cases are where payments differ most from ordinary forms. A payment timeout means the gateway did not respond in time, so the merchant does not know the outcome; the correct behavior is to treat the result as unknown and reconcile later rather than assuming failure, because the charge may have gone through. A network or callback failure means the asynchronous confirmation webhook did not arrive, so the system must poll or reconcile to discover the true status. The user closing the browser mid-payment must not leave money in limbo; the server-side transaction state is the source of truth, not the browser. The single most critical case is payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails: the gateway charged the customer, but the success response or webhook never reached the merchant. If the merchant naively retries the charge, the customer is billed twice; if it marks the order failed, the customer paid for nothing. The only correct design is idempotency plus reconciliation.

Duplicate-transaction handling is the heart of correctness. Because retries happen automatically on timeouts and network blips, the same logical payment can be submitted multiple times. An idempotency key, a unique identifier the client attaches to the payment intent, lets the gateway recognize a repeat and return the original result instead of charging again. The gateway stores the key with the first outcome, so any resend with the same key is a no-op that echoes the first response. Refund cases cover full refunds, which reverse the exact amount, and partial refunds, which reverse part and leave the rest, with the invariant that total refunded never exceeds the captured amount and that refunds are themselves idempotent. Currency conversion cases confirm the correct rate is applied, rounding uses the correct scale with no floating-point error, and the charged and settled currencies are recorded. Transaction-status-mismatch cases confirm that when the merchant's record and the gateway's record disagree, reconciliation resolves to the gateway as the authority on whether money moved.

The reason idempotency and duplicate handling matter more than UI validation is risk asymmetry. A UI validation bug produces an annoying but recoverable user error. A duplicate-charge bug moves real money wrongly, triggers chargebacks, regulatory exposure, and loss of trust, and it happens precisely in the common, unavoidable conditions of timeouts and retries. The senior nuance is that you cannot eliminate retries, so you must make them safe: every mutating payment operation carries an idempotency key, the server deduplicates on that key, and a reconciliation job periodically compares merchant and gateway ledgers to catch and heal any mismatch. Testing therefore must include sending the same idempotency key twice and asserting a single charge, simulating a dropped confirmation and asserting reconciliation converges, and simulating a mid-flight browser close and asserting the server state is authoritative.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When Priya pays through the National Bank of India gateway, a network blip can cause the client to resend the same payment, and without protection she would be charged twice. This is exactly the idempotency-key and duplicate-handling case.

Problem 2 — Sometimes the bank charges her but the confirmation is lost, so the merchant does not know the payment succeeded. The server-side transaction state must be the source of truth and reconciliation must heal the mismatch. This is exactly the payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails case.

Problem 3 — Declines such as insufficient balance, expired card, and wrong CVV must leave balances untouched, and refunds including partial refunds must never exceed the captured amount. These are the financial-correctness invariants.

In the mini-project we model a payment gateway that enforces idempotency, records authoritative transaction state, and supports refunds with the capped-amount invariant, plus a test suite that exercises success, declines, duplicates, lost confirmation, and partial refund. We define a `PaymentResult`, a `PaymentGateway` keyed by idempotency key with declines and refunds, and a `PaymentTestSuite`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya's account with two hundred fifty thousand rupees, a good card, and a suite covering success, duplicate, declines, lost confirmation, and partial refund.

Step 1: The success case charges fifty thousand with idempotency key one. The gateway debits the payer, records reference TXN-1 as the authoritative outcome, and returns CAPTURED.

Step 2: The duplicate case resends key one. The gateway sees the key already exists, so it echoes the original result and does not charge again; the balance stays at two hundred thousand, proving idempotency.

Step 3: The decline cases use a fresh gateway each time and confirm an expired card, a wrong CVV, and insufficient balance are all refused with the balance untouched.

Step 4: The lost-confirmation case charges one thousand with key-X, then the client, having never received the confirmation, retries with the same key-X. The gateway recognizes the key and does not double-charge, so the balance drops by exactly one thousand.

Step 5: The partial-refund case captures twenty thousand, refunds five thousand successfully, then attempts to refund twenty thousand more, which would exceed the captured amount and is rejected, proving the refund-cap invariant.

Final output:


sections.s6_takeaway:
When I test a payment gateway I keep one principle front of mind: this moves real money, so financial correctness and reliability matter far more than cosmetics. My cases start with the success path, a valid payment debits the payer, credits the merchant, records a transaction with a unique reference, and returns captured. Then I cover declines, insufficient balance, invalid or expired card, and wrong CVV, each with the invariant that a declined payment leaves balances completely untouched. Then come the reliability cases that make payments special: a timeout where the result is unknown and must be reconciled rather than assumed failed, a network or callback webhook failure that requires polling or reconciliation, the user closing the browser mid-payment where the server state is authoritative not the browser, and the single most dangerous case, the payment succeeding at the gateway while the confirmation back to the merchant is lost. I also cover duplicate payment requests, full and partial refunds with the invariant that total refunded never exceeds the captured amount, currency conversion with correct rounding and no floating-point error, and transaction-status mismatches where the gateway is the authority on whether money actually moved.

The reason idempotency and duplicate handling matter more than UI validation is risk asymmetry. A UI validation bug is annoying but recoverable; a duplicate-charge bug moves real money wrongly, causes chargebacks and regulatory exposure, and it happens in exactly the routine conditions of timeouts and retries that you cannot eliminate. So the design must make retries safe: every mutating payment carries an idempotency key, the gateway stores the first outcome against that key and returns it unchanged on any resend, and a reconciliation job compares the merchant and gateway ledgers to detect and heal mismatches. My tests therefore send the same key twice and assert a single charge, simulate a dropped confirmation and assert the retry does not double-charge, and assert refunds are capped and idempotent too.

At the National Bank of India I tested exactly this and caught a case where a timeout caused the client to retry without an idempotency key, which would have double-charged customers on slow network days; I made the idempotency key mandatory and added the reconciliation check. Being able to enumerate these money-correctness and reliability cases and to explain why idempotency beats UI validation in importance is what shows an interviewer I understand that in payments the quiet, common failure, charged but not confirmed, is the one that actually loses money and trust.

answers.question: What test-design techniques do you apply to reduce case count while keeping coverage (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, state transition testing, pairwise/combinatorial), and how do they help you choose which inputs to test?
answers.shortTitle: Test-design techniques to reduce case count while keeping coverage

s1_definition.profdef: Test-design techniques are systematic methods for selecting a small, high-value set of test cases that covers the important behavior of a system without exhaustively testing every input. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes that the system treats the same, so one representative per class suffices. Boundary value analysis tests the edges of those classes, where bugs cluster. Decision tables enumerate combinations of conditions and their expected actions, exposing rule gaps. State transition testing covers an entity's states and the legal and illegal transitions between them. Pairwise or combinatorial testing covers all pairs of parameter values with far fewer cases than the full cross-product. Together they let a tester justify why a handful of cases gives strong coverage instead of guessing.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India accepts transfer amounts from one rupee to one hundred thousand rupees. Testing every single amount is impossible, so a smart tester groups amounts into "too low," "valid," and "too high," and tests one from each group; that is equivalence partitioning. Then the tester checks the exact edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, one hundred thousand and one, because bugs love boundaries; that is boundary value analysis. When loan approval depends on several yes-or-no conditions like income, credit score, and age, the tester lays out all the combinations in a grid to be sure every rule is covered; that is a decision table. When a loan moves through applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, the tester checks every allowed and forbidden move; that is state transition testing. And when a form has many dropdowns, the tester covers every pair of choices instead of every combination; that is pairwise testing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Equivalence partitioning picks one input per class, boundary value analysis tests the edges, decision tables cover condition combinations, state transition testing covers legal and illegal moves, and pairwise testing covers all value pairs, so you get strong coverage with few cases and can justify every one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Test-design techniques are systematic methods for selecting a small, high-value set of test cases that covers the important behavior of a system without exhaustively testing every input. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes that the system treats the same, so one representative per class suffices. Boundary value analysis tests the edges of those classes, where bugs cluster. Decision tables enumerate combinations of conditions and their expected actions, exposing rule gaps. State transition testing covers an entity's states and the legal and illegal transitions between them. Pairwise or combinatorial testing covers all pairs of parameter values with far fewer cases than the full cross-product. Together they let a tester justify why a handful of cases gives strong coverage instead of guessing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India accepts transfer amounts from one rupee to one hundred thousand rupees. Testing every single amount is impossible, so a smart tester groups amounts into "too low," "valid," and "too high," and tests one from each group; that is equivalence partitioning. Then the tester checks the exact edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, one hundred thousand and one, because bugs love boundaries; that is boundary value analysis. When loan approval depends on several yes-or-no conditions like income, credit score, and age, the tester lays out all the combinations in a grid to be sure every rule is covered; that is a decision table. When a loan moves through applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, the tester checks every allowed and forbidden move; that is state transition testing. And when a form has many dropdowns, the tester covers every pair of choices instead of every combination; that is pairwise testing.

**One line to remember:** Equivalence partitioning picks one input per class, boundary value analysis tests the edges, decision tables cover condition combinations, state transition testing covers legal and illegal moves, and pairwise testing covers all value pairs, so you get strong coverage with few cases and can justify every one.

sections.s2_technical:
Equivalence partitioning is the foundation. You divide each input into partitions, ranges or categories that the system is expected to treat identically, and then test just one representative value from each partition, because if the code handles one member of a class correctly it almost certainly handles the rest the same way. For a transfer amount valid between one and one hundred thousand, the partitions are below range, in range, and above range, plus invalid types such as negative or non-numeric, giving a handful of cases instead of thousands. The payoff is a dramatic reduction in cases with little loss of coverage, as long as your partitions truly reflect how the system behaves.

Boundary value analysis complements partitioning by attacking the edges, because off-by-one errors and wrong comparison operators cluster exactly at boundaries. For the one-to-one-hundred-thousand range you test zero, one, one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand and one, and often also the just-inside and just-outside values. Many defects that partitioning alone would miss are caught here, because a bug like using less-than instead of less-than-or-equal only shows at the boundary.

Decision tables handle combinational logic where the output depends on several conditions. You list each condition as a row, enumerate the combinations as columns, and record the expected action for each, which both generates test cases and reveals missing or contradictory rules in the specification. For loan approval depending on sufficient income, acceptable credit score, and minimum age, the table makes explicit what happens for every true-and-false combination, so you neither miss a rule nor duplicate one. You can collapse infeasible or don't-care combinations to keep the table compact.

State transition testing applies when an entity has a lifecycle. You model the states, the events that cause transitions, the legal transitions, and importantly the illegal ones, and you design cases to cover each transition at least once plus attempts at forbidden transitions to confirm they are rejected. For a loan moving applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, you test each valid step and also that you cannot, say, disburse an application that was never approved. Pairwise or combinatorial testing addresses the explosion when many parameters each have several values; testing the full cross-product is infeasible, but most defects are triggered by the interaction of just two parameters, so covering all pairs of values catches the large majority of combination bugs with a small fraction of the cases. Tools generate the minimal pairwise set for you.

The senior nuance is that these techniques are complementary, not alternatives, and choosing inputs is about risk and behavior, not mechanical application. You partition first to shrink the space, apply boundary analysis to the partitions where edges matter, use a decision table where several conditions combine into an action, use state transition testing where an entity has a meaningful lifecycle, and use pairwise where many independent parameters would otherwise explode. The real skill, and what an interviewer listens for, is that you can look at a feature and say which technique fits and why, and then justify your chosen case set as deliberate coverage rather than a random pile of examples.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India transfer accepts amounts from one to one hundred thousand rupees, and testing every amount is impossible. The bank needs a principled way to pick a few amounts that represent all behaviors. This is exactly equivalence partitioning plus boundary value analysis.

Problem 2 — Loan approval depends on three yes-or-no conditions, income, credit score, and age, and the bank must be sure every combination has a defined outcome. This is exactly a decision table.

Problem 3 — A loan has a lifecycle, and some transitions must be forbidden. This is exactly state transition testing.

In the mini-project we build a small library that applies each technique to a banking rule and prints the generated cases, so the demo shows how few cases give strong coverage. We define a `TransferValidator` and `LoanDecision` as the logic under test, and a `TestDesignDemo` that derives partition, boundary, decision-table, and state-transition cases and runs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer validator with a one-to-one-hundred-thousand range, a three-condition loan rule, and a loan state machine.

Step 1: Equivalence partitioning runs one representative per class, a negative amount from the invalid class, fifty thousand from the valid class, and two hundred thousand from the above class, covering all three behaviors in three cases instead of thousands.

Step 2: Boundary value analysis runs the edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand and one, catching any off-by-one in the comparison operators.

Step 3: The decision table enumerates all eight true-and-false combinations of income, credit, and age, confirming approval happens only when all three hold and every other combination is rejected, with no rule gap.

Step 4: State transition testing confirms the legal moves applied-to-approved and approved-to-disbursed are allowed, and the illegal move applied-to-disbursed is correctly rejected.

Step 5: The pairwise note shows that three parameters with three values each have twenty-seven full combinations, but roughly nine cases cover all value pairs, catching most interaction bugs with a third of the cases.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Test-design techniques are how I get strong coverage from a small, justified set of cases instead of either testing exhaustively, which is impossible, or guessing randomly, which misses bugs. Equivalence partitioning is my starting point: I divide each input into classes the system treats the same and test one representative per class, so a transfer amount valid from one to one hundred thousand collapses to a below-range case, an in-range case, and an above-range case. Boundary value analysis then attacks the edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand and one, because off-by-one errors and wrong comparison operators cluster exactly there and partitioning alone would miss them. Decision tables handle logic where several conditions combine into an action: I list the conditions, enumerate the combinations, and record the expected action, which both generates cases and exposes missing or contradictory rules, which is how I cover a loan approval that depends on income, credit, and age. State transition testing applies when an entity has a lifecycle: I cover each legal transition and also attempt the illegal ones, so I confirm a loan cannot be disbursed without approval. And pairwise or combinatorial testing tames the explosion when many parameters each have several values, because most defects come from the interaction of just two parameters, so covering all value pairs catches the majority of combination bugs with a fraction of the full cross-product.

The key point I make is that these are complementary, not alternatives, and that choosing inputs is about risk and behavior. I partition to shrink the space, apply boundaries where edges matter, use a decision table where conditions combine, use state transition where a lifecycle exists, and use pairwise where parameters would otherwise explode.

At the National Bank of India this discipline paid off directly. For the transfer amount field I replaced a sprawling, ad hoc list of amounts with a tight partition-plus-boundary set and immediately caught a defect where the maximum used less-than instead of less-than-or-equal, so exactly one hundred thousand was wrongly rejected, a bug only the boundary case would reveal. For loan approval I built a decision table that exposed a missing rule for the borderline-age case the spec had not defined. Being able to name each technique, say which feature it fits, and justify my case set as deliberate coverage rather than a random pile of examples is exactly what shows an interviewer I design tests like an engineer rather than writing whatever comes to mind.
